I am pretty new to Bitcoin. I understand how the blockchain works, etc... but I can't figure this part out.

I have a computer with a fresh Linux distro, I generate a paperwallet completely offline. I print it off and begin giving people the public address to receive payments. How does the Bitcoin network even know this address exists? How do they know the private key that unlocks it?

Does sending BTC to an address automatically create it on the network? If so, how does the network know what private key will unlock it? Hopefully all of you who are much smarter than me can unlock this silly mystery to me. Thanks!
When I generate offline paper wallets, how does my public address to receive Bitcoins get onto the network?

Sending BTC to that address will put it on the network. The blockchain contains transactions with input and output addresses. To spend money you create a transaction and then sign it with the private key (or keys) that correspond to the input addresses.

Can you explain the method of signing a transaction? The network must be sure that it's signed with a valid private key so how is it determined to be valid without allowing it to be read - and therefore making it possible to steal somebody's private key?

That's the magic of public key encryption. Essentially you encrypt a hash of the transaction with your private key. A node on the network can verify the transaction by first using the public key to decrypt the encrypted hash and comparing it with the hash it's calculated itself.

As others have replied, the network doesn't know, and doesn't need to know.

The best... or worst... is that the reverse is true: someone could also send bitcoins to an address that doesn't exist (in the sense that there is no private key associated). There is a checksum at the end of each address to prevent simple typos from being accepted as valid, and addresses have a few restrictions on their format (allowed letters), but if you really want you can generate a valid address, without knowing if there is any private key able to unlock it. Any coins sent to it are basically lost, unspendable, in a blackhole.

This is the case of the 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSend59kuE "address". It exists on the blockchain, some people "burnt" their money sending it (a few) satoshis, but nobody has the private key.
